newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Two U.N. workers killed in fresh Rwanda violence.
newsitem.headline: Two U.N. workers killed in fresh Rwanda violence.

text.p: The U.N. food agency on Wednesday reported two Rwandan staffers and relatives, including a child, shot dead in northwestern Rwanda.
World Food Programme spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said field officer Didace Nkezagera was killed at the weekend in his home in Ruhengeri region with his wife, child and another relative.
The body of a second Rwandan employee, clerk Jean de Dieu Murwanashyaka, was found in a forest near Ruhengeri on Tuesday. He had been shot in the head.

They were the first killings of aid workers since a series of brutal and unexplained murders earlier this year, including the killing of three Spanish relief workers in January and five U.N. human rights workers in February.
The WFP condemed "these first brutal murders of WFP staff in Rwanda" and demanded an investigation, Berthiaume said.
Ruhengeri, near Zaire's border, is populated predominantly by Hutus, Rwanda's majority tribe, and has been the scene of clashes between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels.
The WFP did not identify the communal origin of the muredered aid workers.
Aid staff in Rwanda said the victims were Hutu. They said the WFP field officer was a recent Hutu returnee from Zaire who had recently been questioned by soldiers on his agency's work.
The Hutu clerk was arrested by troops and had not been seen since, they added.
In Ruhengeri, the WFP was feeding 100,000 Hutu returnees, many of them collectively accused of killing by Tutsi survivors. Some had accused the WFP of feeding only Hutus, aid workers said.
Amnesty International has charged Rwandan troops with unlawful executions of civilians in reprisal for attacks on government soldiers and then saying civilians were killed in cross-fire.
Communal tensions in Rwanda have risen with the return home of more than 800,000 Hutu refugees from Zaire since late last year, among them Hutu militiamen who have stepped up their rebellion.
They fled in fear of reprisal for 1994's Hutu-led genocide of more than half a million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Aid agencies have expressed renewed concern at the upsurge in violence, which prevents them from carrying out investigations into abuses and killings.
They say large swathes of Rwanda have become no-go areas, including Ruhengeri which has absorbed large numbers of Hutu returnees.

"According to our office in Kigali, 25 percent of Rwanda is completely out of bounds to us and 50 percent is only accessible with an army escort," U.N. children's agency UNICEF spokesman Patrick McCormick said.
The majority of more than 80 U.N. human rights observers stationed in Rwanda are confined mostly to the capital Kigali since the February killing of their five colleagues.
The U.N. refugee agency, which has airlifted more than 50,000 Rwandan Hutus from Zaire to Kigali in recent months, says it has been unable to monitor the bulk of the returnees.
